chapter_theme: The youth who joins a Vidyadhara woman is seized by her brother and dropped in the forest, where a sage rescues him and foretells his rule and marriage; he visits his parents, flies to Sridharaloka and meets a Vidyadhara who tells of a king's daughter whose dream a sage reads as a sign of his coming.

cast.role: Udayanan's son, called by titles such as காளை in these verses
the Vidyadhara brother of the woman, who seizes the pair
the Vidyadhara woman who joins the youth and gives up her art
the sage who foretells the youth's rule and later reads the dream
the youth's mother, whose grief he soothes (not named in 274)
the young Vidyadhara who worships the youth's feet and names Gandharvapuram
the Vidyadhara king of Gandharvapuram, father of Nagadattai
Nilavekan's daughter who has the dream

263.reading: Pollen drifts down over the earth like a peacock's tail spread in the cloud-dark hour, and the proud youth, seeing the girl, finds the way clear of fault and joins with her.
263.nuance: The first two lines are a scene-setting image whose syntax is broken in the edition (மாத விப்பொதும்); the girl is not named, and she may be the Vidyadhara woman of the next verses.
263.event: The youth, having judged that no fault bars it, unites with the girl.

264.reading: On another day the lord sees the flower-haired woman asleep and, as she comes to his side, she speaks to him at length, asking who he is, a stranger.
264.nuance: The verse does not say who is asleep and who speaks; it is read here as the maiden coming to the youth, though the sleeper may be the youth's own bride.
264.event: A woman asks the youth who he is and talks with him at length.

265.reading: The generous youth asks the woman to show him the form she likes best; she does, and he joins with her while Mara's arrows urge him on.
265.nuance: The shape-showing implies she is a Vidyadhara who can change form; the verse does not say so.
265.event: The woman shows the shape he asked for, and the youth joins with her.

266.reading: Manasavegan, master of the Vidyadhara arts, cannot find his sister, learns from the court that she has gone, comes in anger and seizes both.
266.nuance: His anger is the wronged brother's: the verse treats the pair's union as an offence to be punished, with no word for the woman's own will.
266.event: Manasavegan learns his sister has left and seizes her and the youth.

267.reading: Manasavegan leaves the youth in the sky and goes down; the woman of the dark hair gives up her Vidyadhara art, and the youth falls into the forest.
267.nuance: The verse does not say why the youth falls, whether her art held him up or the brother let go; the readings turn on the doubtful wording of line 2.
267.event: Manasavegan abandons the youth in mid-air, his sister drops her art, and the youth falls into the forest.

268.reading: As the fallen youth lies like a leaf of bamboo, the great sage, the beloved father of the bright-speared king of Vatsa, who is to cast off future births, sees him.
268.nuance: The sage is called the father of the Vatsa king; the verse does not say he is the same as the Sumitra of verse 281, and an earlier life of the king is possible.
268.event: The sage sees the fallen youth.

269.reading: Knowing by his power of enlightenment what has happened, the sage goes out in love, names the youth and his father, and the youth comes and bows.
269.nuance: போதி (line 1) is read as the sage's wisdom or insight; the word is rare in this sense.
269.event: The sage says the youth's name and his father's name, and the youth bows to him.

270.reading: The youth asks the sage how he knows his father and himself, and the sage, in due order, tells who they are; the youth listens with deepening feeling and then hears one thing more.
270.event: The youth asks how the sage knew them; the sage explains.

271.reading: The sage says the sages' word is that he will conquer and rule the Vidyadhara cities and that his state is unfailing; the great ascetic tells it truly.
271.event: The sage foretells that the youth will rule the Vidyadhara cities.

claims.claim: the word of true sages foretells a ruler's future and does not fail

272.reading: The sage tells him the whole realm on the silver mountain will come under his feet with wealth beyond reproach, and the youth listens.
272.event: The sage promises the youth the Vidyadhara realm of Vellimalai.

273.reading: The youth leaves the great ascetic, goes to the city, and after seeing his father and mother, tells them lovingly how his misfortune ended and his beloved was parted from him.
273.nuance: The speaker of the last line is called அன்னோன் ('that one'); the verse names no wife, so the beloved's parting is either from the Vidyadhara woman or from his wedded wife.
273.event: The youth rejoins his parents and tells them of the end of his trouble and of his parted wife.

274.reading: He soothes his mother's grief by reporting what the true ascetic said, mounts the sky-going chariot, and goes happily.
274.event: The youth tells his mother what the ascetic said, ends her grief, and mounts a sky-chariot.

275.reading: With love the chariot goes along the sky-road southwards to Sridharaloka on the Vidyadhara ridge, and the youth, told to rest by a fair pond, stays gladly.
275.event: The youth flies south to Sridharaloka and rests by a pond.

276.reading: He stands at the long bank, bathes without shaking, anoints himself with fragrant water and sits there; a young man seeing his feet worships them.
276.event: The youth bathes and sits at the pond, and a young man worships his feet.

277.reading: The lord asks the young man who he is, and the cool-tongued Vidyadhara says his city is Gandharvapuram on the hard-to-reach hill.
277.event: The youth asks the stranger who he is; the stranger names Gandharvapuram.

278.reading: The Vidyadhara king Nilavekan has a fair daughter, Nagadattai of fame, and the flower-vine Manmatha-vilasai, as another daughter.
278.nuance: Whether Nagadattai and Anangavilasai are two daughters or one woman with two names cannot be fixed from the fragmentary syntax of lines 3 and 4.
278.event: The stranger names the king's daughters Nagadattai and Anangavilasai.

279.reading: Asleep on a bed with bee-sung garlands, the sweet-voiced girl dreams that a curse of power, lion and fish, rose from the earth in her lover's company.
279.nuance: The dream is told in bare images (சிங்கம், மீன், சாபம்) whose referents the verse does not give; it is the sage's reply in 282 that makes them a sign.
279.event: The girl dreams of a lion and a fish and a curse that rises from the earth.

280.reading: In the dream a creature comes down from the hill and bites the pearl necklace on her breast, then sets a fragrant garland on her with pride; the girl wakes and tells her kin.
280.event: The girl sees a creature take her necklace and crown her with a garland, and tells her kin.

281.reading: The king of the victorious spear hears, goes to the unreachable sage Sumitra, bows at his feet in due form, and asks the ascetic about the good dream.
281.nuance: The sage here is named சுமித்திர, and the Vidyadhara king consults him like the youth's own guide of verse 268; whether they are one person is left open.
281.event: The king hears the dream, goes to the sage Sumitra and asks him to read it.

282.reading: The sage, who has understood, gives grace and says the beloved lord now arriving will wed the king's daughter and, with the disc complete, will rule this earth.
282.event: The sage reads the dream and says the coming youth will marry the king's daughter and rule the earth.

claims.claim: a dream seen by a woman foretells her marriage and her husband's rule

links.note: The sage's reading of the dream in 282 answers the dream the girl tells in 279 and 280.
links.teaches: The dream's lion, fish and curse stay riddles until the sage names a bridegroom and an empire as their meaning, so the reading is the dream's fulfilment.

links.note: Two prophecies by sages, one for the youth's Vidyadhara rule, one for his marriage and earthly rule.
links.teaches: The youth's promised rule is told from his side by one sage and from the bride's side by another, so the two prophecies fit together into a single destiny.

links.note: The youth's fall into the forest in 267 brings the sage's rescue in 268.
links.teaches: The brother's cruelty ends not in the youth's death but in an encounter that sets his future, which turns the fall into the start of his rise.

source_issues: Verses 263 to 282 are heavily corrupt in the edition: the line 'மாத விப்பொதும் பின்மயிற் றோகைபோல்' (263) and the word divisions of 268, 269 and 278 to 280 do not parse cleanly, so the speakers and the person of the sage are partly inferred.
The sage called the father of the Vatsa king (268) and the sage Sumitra (281) may be one person; the verses do not say.
